title: Mogharaja's question (Sn 5)
hookLine: read it: look on the world as empty, and death won't see you
tomorrow: what if you can't follow your teacher anymore, even on foot?

cards: You post something you're proud of. Twenty kind comments, and one that stings. Guess which one gets read nine times.
A student named Mogharaja knew something about waiting on a response. He says he's asked the Buddha twice already and got no answer; the poem doesn't say why.
On the third try he asks: how should a person look on the world, so the king of death doesn't see him? The answer is short enough to carry around all week.

teach.h: LOOK ON THE WORLD AS EMPTY.
teach.b: The Buddha says, in Mogharaja's question: look on the world as empty, Mogharaja, always mindful. Root out the view of a self, and so cross over death. Whoever looks on the world like that, the king of death doesn't see.
Empty doesn't mean worthless, or that nothing matters. In another sutta, the Buddha's attendant Ananda asks exactly that: in what sense is the world called empty?

teach.h: EMPTY OF A SELF AND WHAT'S MINE.
teach.b: Because, the Buddha says, it is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self. The eyes, the sights, the comments, the feelings they bring up: real, all of them, and none of them a solid, fixed me or mine.
So here's what that gives you this week.

teach.h: NO STATUE OUT OF THE STING.
teach.b: When the sting lands, there's a habit of building a little statue out of it: this is who I am now, the one they called amateur. Looking on it as empty is noticing the statue isn't there. A comment came.
A feeling came. Both are passing through. Nothing solid got hit.
And the king of death? In these poems, death finds what we fasten onto as self. Look lightly, the poem says, and there's nothing for it to grab.
You can still care about the work, the people, the day.
You just don't have to build a monument to every word.

how: Buddhist teachers in different schools teach emptiness, the world as empty of a fixed self, and Mogharaja's question is one text read for it; meditators practice by noticing experiences as passing, not as 'me' or 'mine'.

o: a monk's question about which robe color to wear
a student's question: how should one look on the world?
a king's question about how to rule an empty land

p: asked twice, answered the third time
how to look on the world
of a self and what is a self's

s: look on the world as empty means nothing matters, so don't care
empty means empty of a self and of what belongs to a self; you can still care about the work and the people.
Mogharaja says he had asked twice before getting an answer
the poem has him ask a third time; it doesn't say why the Buddha waited.

games.q: your manager says one critical thing in a long, good review, and it's all you can think about on the drive home. what does Mogharaja's answer point you toward?
o: see the remark and the sting as passing, not a fixed fact about who you are.
decide reviews are empty, so stop caring about your work at all.
replay the remark until you've got a perfect comeback ready.
games.why: the world is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self. the remark is real; it just isn't a statue of you. you can still care about the work.

practice: Choose one thing in front of you, a cup, a shoe, your own hand, and look at it slowly. Notice its parts, its colors, the light on it, its name.
Then see if you can find the one solid thing it is, apart from all that, and let your eyes rest lightly on it while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Mogharaja's question: asked on the third try. How should one look on the world so death doesn't see? As empty of a self, mindfully, with the view of self rooted out.

orig.note: Pali: empty; Sanskrit shunya. Look on the world as sunna.

carryVoice: For the comment that stings: look on it as empty, and keep caring anyway. Sixteen seventy-eight, held lightly.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 5.15 (Mogharajamanavapuccha, Mogharaja's question, in the Parayanavagga)
Samyutta Nikaya 35.85 (Sunna Sutta: the world is empty of self and of what belongs to self)
